newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac under pressure from truckers, EMU debate.
newsitem.headline: Chirac under pressure from truckers, EMU debate.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac is under pressure to break his silence in the face of attacks on his enfeebled government from striking truck drivers and critics of its "strong franc" policy, political sources said on Monday.

Since returning from Japan last week, his only public words have been a televised eulogy for author and culture minister Andre Malraux, who was reburied with republican pomp in the Pantheon of national heroes on Saturday.
If Chirac is concerned about truck drivers blockading the nation's highways and fuel depots to demand higher pay, shorter hours and early retirement, he is keeping it a well-guarded secret.

While the president reaffirmed in Japan his support for the deficit-cutting policies of beleaguered Prime Minister Alain Juppe, whose popularity is at an all-time low, he has carefully stayed aloof from the day-to-day management of the country.

Nor has he responded to last week's call by one of his eminent predecessors, Valery Giscard d'Estaing, for an effective devaluation of the franc, which caused turmoil in the centre-right coalition, jitters on foreign exchange markets and momentary irritation in Franco-German relations.

The government was quick to reject any idea of unhooking the franc from the deutschemark, but political sources said Giscard d'Estaing, father of the European Monetary System, had said aloud what many Chirac supporters think privately -- that a weaker franc is needed to revive growth and employment.

Chirac has not addressed the nation in a policy statement or a television interview since last July 14, and there are growing demands among his own Gaullist supporters that he give a strong political lead to an anxious and gloomy country.

Chirac backers argue that Juppe no longer commands enough respect to remobilise support for government policies. Backbench parliamentarians who fear losing their seats to the Socialist opposition in a 1998 general election are urging the president to reassert his leadership.
"It's high time the boss spoke out and pointed the country in the right direction," one Gaullist official said.

But political sources say Chirac's influential image consultant, Jacques Pilhan, who long served his Socialist predecessor Francois Mitterrand, has advised him to ration his own appearances and wait for an opportune moment.
Pilhan argues there is no point in the president speaking at a time when people are not disposed to listen, or when his intervention would not create a turning point, they say.

In the meantime, his interventions are largely confined to remarks reported by the government spokesman after the weekly cabinet meeting, and comments at news conferences with foreign leaders, neither of which carry the same political weight as a broadcast to the nation.

Chirac's determination to stick to austerity policies necessary to qualify France for a single European currency, despite deepening unpopularity, has led to talk of a reshuffle to breathe new life into Juppe's flagging government.
Education Minister Francois Bayrou hinted in a television interview on Sunday that a reshuffle was under consideration "so that the coalition's composition is reflected in government".
But he said such a change must not be seen as "a sign of weakness" and there must first be an agreement reaffirming the country's direction, Bayrou said.

One of the expected beneficiaries, ex-budget minister Nicolas Sarkozy, suggested a shakeup was not imminent, saying in an RTL radio interview: "My belief is that there's no urgency in reshuffling the cabinet or changing faces."
